title: The Judge Under Trial: Monte Carlo Verification of the Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning Lifecycle
content: The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) as automated evaluators—commonly termed LLM-as-a-Judge—introduces a critical vulnerability: the “right answer, wrong reason” failure mode, where a judge reaches the correct verdict through unsound reasoning that is invisible to standard label-agreement dashboards. Kong et al. [1] propose Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning (RART) to address this, anchoring the judge’s rationale to human judgment via a Meta-Judge and iterative rubric refinement. This paper presents a reproducible Monte Carlo simulation (300 replicates, 40 iterations) that empirically verifies the RART lifecycle against a label-only baseline (Vanilla). We formally model the latent rubric state θ_R = (q_R, b_R), the noisy meta-judge detection layer, the biased reflector update, and the statistical drift monitor. Our results confirm the framework’s central thesis. While Vanilla achieves marginally higher final label accuracy (q_R = 0.956) than RART (q_R = 0.875), its reasoning alignment collapses entirely (b_R = −0.842), whereas RART stabilizes reasoning (b_R = +0.910). Furthermore, the simulation visually exposes the structural vulnerabilities of the framework: Vanilla consumes 2.6× the computational budget (39.4 vs 14.8 iterations) due to the stopping-rule artifact; the standard 2σ drift band produces an unacceptable 11.3% false-alarm rate at K = 3 raters; and the blind-spot leak between shared judge-generator architectures decays only when human oversight (p_H > 0) is present. The simulation serves as both a pedagogical tool and an empirical validation that the LLM judge is an amplifier of human judgment, not a replacement for it.
